text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, the value or not of having what's called your coronary
calcium score measured on a CT scan. It has been a money-maker for years, the
question is whether it's worth doing. A trial of common painkillers comparing their
ability to cause heart attacks. A way to bring down the cost and perhaps increase
the availability of some of the most expensive cancer drugs. And two trials which
suggests that an automated online therapy program for insomnia works, and
there's a strong Australian connection. The person who has led the project for
some years is Lee Ritterband, professor of psychiatry and neurobehavioural
sciences at the University of Virginia. Welcome to the Health Report.

Lee Ritterband: Thanks for having me.

Norman Swan: So how do you define insomnia?

Lee Ritterband: Difficulty falling asleep, waking up in the middle of the night not
being able to get back to sleep, waking too early in the morning or just not feeling
like you've had a good night's sleep.

Norman Swan: But the message here is that you are bothered by it, because
some people might have the same sort of issues but they are not bothered by it.

Lee Ritterband: That's right, absolutely.

Norman Swan: And where did the idea that cognitive behavioural therapy might
work for insomnia…? Because you'd think, well, you're waking up so why bother?
What's going to make a difference to your sleep if you are told to think differently
about it?

Lee Ritterband: Well, cognitive behavioural therapy is a general approach that
actually has been found to be pretty efficacious in a number of different areas,
and insomnia and sleep happen to be one of them that it is particularly good at
addressing. It focuses on how we think and how we feel and the connection
between the two. And what we find is that a lot of the difficulties that people have
with their sleep are wrapped up in how they are thinking about their sleep and the
anxiety that revolves around their sleep, and so there is some cognitive work that
focuses on thinking differently about how we sleep. And the behaviour piece is
 
really focused on implementing certain rules and guidelines and strategies that
can improve the actual process of sleep.

Norman Swan: So-called sleep hygiene, that's the bed is just for sleeping and
sex, and not for working and not for watching television, and go to bed at the
same time each night and don't have coffee before you go to bed and that sort of
thing.

Lee Ritterband: That's right. Actually you combine both the sleep hygiene as
well as the stimulus control strategies. There are three areas in there, there's
sleep hygiene which is a lot of the things people already know; don't drink coffee
close to bed, don't exercise close to bed, some of those issues. There are the
stimulus control techniques that we are trying to disconnect the body's tendency
to be awake when in bed and not sleep. And so there is an attempt to modify that
through some rules, which is what the stimulus control rules are.

And then there is this third piece which is sleep restriction, which is a bit
paradoxical in the sense that we actually restrict people's sleep initially in order to
improve the efficiency of their sleep. And so what we see is that a lot of folks
come in with really poor sleep efficiency. And we calculate sleep efficiency by
looking at what percentage of time are people asleep when they are in bed. So if
I'm sleeping for five hours a night but I'm in bed for 10 hours, then I have a 50%
sleep efficiency, and we really want to get people up over 85%. And to do that we
will often encourage a shorter period of time of being in bed to sleep as a way of
consolidating sleep during that period.

Norman Swan: And the stimulus control?

Lee Ritterband: The stimulus control are the rules that you were starting to
mention before, you know, only use the bed for sleep and sex, don't watch
television or do other things in bed, you get out of bed if you are not asleep within
20 minutes. All of those rules are put in place in order to break the connection of
being awake when in bed.

Norman Swan: You've been one of the international pioneers, along with Helen
Christensen at the Black Dog and others, of online therapy. So you instituted this
as an online piece where you didn't actually have a therapist, you did this as part
of an online program called SHUTi. Just tell us a little bit about this study.
 
Lee Ritterband: The study was looking at the use of this online program SHUTi,
and following people over a period of a year to see how well does the
intervention…and this is a fully automated, interactive, tailored program, there is
no human support involved in it. And we wanted to see if we gave this to people,
if we had them use it, how well would it work over a longer period of time. And we
looked at people right after they used it, at six months after they used it and then
at one year to see how they were doing.

Norman Swan: And how did they go?

Lee Ritterband: Great, just really strong, positive, robust outcomes. We've done
a number of studies with SHUTi now over the last few years, and this study was
particularly of interest because we were really opening it up to a lot of different
kinds of people, people who had already different issues that were going on,
psychiatric issues like depression or anxiety as well as medical problems,
whether they had asthma or cancer or other medical problems. Over 50% of the
people who were in this trial had one or both of those kinds of issues. And so we
really wanted to see if SHUTi worked in this real-world setting. And the findings
were as strong as we've ever seen.

Norman Swan: So, faster to sleep, longer sleeping times, that sort of thing?

Lee Ritterband: Yes, faster to sleep, not being awake as long in the middle of
the night, having much improved sleep. In fact over half of the group who got
SHUTi were what we call treatment remitters, they were not having any insomnia
anymore at one year.

Norman Swan: And you did another study with Helen Christensen at the Black
Dog and others at the ANU and Sydney University looking at people with
depression. What was the findings there?

Lee Ritterband: Yes, that was a fantastic study. We recruited over 1,000 people
in Australia, and everybody in that trial had insomnia but were also at risk for
major depression. And what we found was that if we treated those who had
insomnia and were at risk for major depression, that we could not only
significantly improve their sleep, which we did, but we also significantly
decreased their depressive aspect, they were not feeling as depressed anymore.
Insomnia and depression definitely are comorbid, they often come together.
 
Sometimes depression leads to the insomnia, sometimes the insomnia leads to
the depression, and oftentimes they are just comorbid, meaning that they happen
around the same time.

Norman Swan: You're not the only program that offers cognitive behavioural
therapy for insomnia. How does yours rate with the others?

Lee Ritterband: Yes, there are some other programs, and there are some that
have good data. But the concern is that people who are looking to consume
these programs, is to really make sure that the program is that they want to buy
or to use have some real evidence base behind them, but nothing comes close to
the robustness of the data that we see with SHUTi.

Norman Swan: And if you want it in Australia you can get it via the Black Dog
Institute?

Lee Ritterband: You can, you can go to the Black Dog Institute's webpage and
they should have a box there, a link there that you can select to go and get
SHUTi right from there.

Norman Swan: And there is a charge for SHUTi, by the way. Lee Ritterbrand is
professor of psychiatry and neurobehavioural sciences at the University of
Virginia.

And you're listening to the Health Report here on RN, at ABC News Radio and
CBC Radio across Canada. I'm Norman Swan.

Some of the commonest painkillers bought across the counter are called non-
steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or NSAIDs, medications like ibuprofen or
naproxen, their trade names are Nurofen or Naprosyn. There's been a suspicion
that in some people they may increase the risk of a heart attack, particularly a
newer supposedly lower risk NSAID called celecoxib, Celebrex. Well, now a
huge trial has been published comparing these three NSAIDs and their heart
risks, and one of the authors was Professor Neville Yeomans of Western Sydney
University and the Austin Hospital in Melbourne and he joins me in the studio
now. Welcome Neville.

Neville Yeomans: Glad to be with you Norman.
 
Norman Swan: It's a huge study.

Neville Yeomans: Yes, it took a long while, it's been a lot of work, but at the end
of the day I think it has been worth it.

Norman Swan: So let's just talk about why do NSAIDs, in theory, increase the
risk of a heart attack?

Neville Yeomans: You know, that in itself, I think that theory is pretty muddied.
But more to the point they did appear that they do increase the risk a little bit. If I
just wind back a tiny bit, the problem with the NSAIDs that I think most people
know is they do cause some damage to the gut and can cause a bleeding ulcer.
So when it was worked out that there was one molecule they blocked that is bad
for the stomach and the other one they block is good for the pain and
inflammation, that's when the selective COX-2 NSAIDs were developed.

Norman Swan: And that's what celecoxib is.

Neville Yeomans: That's right.

Norman Swan: And infamously there was a sister drug called rofecoxib.

Neville Yeomans: Right, and you are bringing me really to what was the main
source of the concern. In a big study…because these drugs seemed generally
pretty safe and were likely to cause less ulcers and less bleeding, both Celebrex
and rofecoxib were trialled to try to prevent bowel cancer. The irony is that both
of them showed benefit in that. But after about 18 months in two of the studies
and not the third there began to be slightly more heart attacks. And it got to the
extent with rofecoxib of being about twice as much. It could have been chance
but it seemed unlikely to be chance, so there was suddenly concern about the
whole family of them.

Norman Swan: And there was an element of hiding the results, and rofecoxib
ended up getting taken off the market.

Neville Yeomans: Some of that is true actually, and it was perhaps almost
surprising that Celebrex remained, although it did appear to have rather different
properties. And what we also know now is that probably all of the NSAIDs slightly
 
increase the risk of a heart attack, and we didn't know that because in the old
days they were never tested to the same level.

Norman Swan: So Pfizer, the drug company, funded this study to compare
Celebrex against two other common ones, ibuprofen and naproxen.

Neville Yeomans: Yes, I think they really were planning to look into this anyway,
in fact I know they were, with a study they didn't go ahead with. But then the
Food and Drug Administration in the States said, look, this is a concern, and so
they mandated the study, and Pfizer then had no choice. It's been a big and
expensive exercise.

Norman Swan: And you were independent of the drug company?

Neville Yeomans: We were. In fact the steering committee…in fact interestingly
every member of the executive committee every year signed an affidavit that they
would take no finance from any maker of any NSAIDs.

Norman Swan: So what did you find?

Neville Yeomans: Well, the key thing was; was there going to be difference in
cardiovascular deaths?

Norman Swan: And these are people with rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis,
they were taking it for pain relief for their arthritis?

Neville Yeomans: Absolutely, they had proven that they needed it, they had
been on it for at least six months, it was judged that they needed to continue with
it for up to three or four years, and they were told that one of the drugs might
increase their risk of a heart attack. So that was brave people to tackle it. The
primary endpoint was just that; was there an increased risk of cardiac death,
acute myocardial infarction, that is heart attack, and acute stroke? It was the first
time I've been involved with what's called a non-inferiority trial where you start
from the very beginning to plan the study on the assumption that there will be a
difference and you want to find out if there is. Normally you are doing things in
the reverse order. The answer, to cut to the chase, was that perhaps almost to
the surprise of some of us there was no difference between the three NSAIDs in
cardiac risk. There was actually a trend to slightly less on the one that is safer for
 
the stomach. And perhaps most importantly there was a one-third reduction in
all-cause mortality that was statistically significant.

Norman Swan: So was that from bowel cancer or what?

Neville Yeomans: No, most of them will have been cardiovascular, renal,
GI…look, I can't actually tell you the full breakdown of the deaths.

Norman Swan: But it could have been a few things.

Neville Yeomans: Oh yes, there would have been others.

Norman Swan: But there have been other studies which show that ibuprofen
does raise the risk of…so in other words what you didn't answer was if you didn't
take any NSAIDs, would you have had a lower risk of a heart attack or stroke?

Neville Yeomans: That's a really good question, and to really answer it well
would be a randomised trial where you put somebody on a placebo for three
years who had an increased risk of heart disease and had bad joints, and no one
could ever do that, so we have to fall back on epidemiologic studies. And the
epidemiology suggests there is probably a slight increase with all of them.
There's one study that is just under review at the moment from Québec province
where they've got wonderful data linkage that said that the increase in risk…it's
probably a bit unfair for me to say this because it hasn't gone through a full peer
review, but I've got this far to say it looked like about a 10% increase with
celecoxib and a little bit more with most of the others. But these aren't poison,
this is not like smoking and lung cancer.

Norman Swan: What's a person to do? They've got arthritis and let's say they've
got high cholesterol, the doctor has told them they are at high risk of heart
disease. Is it safe to go and buy one of these off the counter?

Neville Yeomans: Look, I think based on what we have found, if it were me I
would be inclined to take one of them by prescription, that means your doctor is
looking after you closely. Oh, I should say that all of these patients were taking
an antiulcer drug which adds a little expense but also made the whole thing
safer. So if they've got bad joints they've got to do something for pain, and if they
can't exercise that's bad for the heart. I think it's important to control pain.
 
Norman Swan: So just get it in balance. And the celecoxib had lower risk of
stomach problems but it wasn't so good for pain relief, that was the other thing.

Neville Yeomans: Yes, maybe so. There was a slight difference against one of
the other two drugs and not the other, so yes, fair comment.

Norman Swan: Neville, thank you very much for joining us.

Neville Yeomans: It's been a pleasure.

Norman Swan: Neville Yeomans who is director of research at the Austin
Hospital in Melbourne.

The Australian healthcare system and often you and me as consumers spend a
fortune on testing to see whether we have heart disease or are at risk of a heart
attack. One such test is called a coronary calcium score and involves a CT scan
of the heart looking at how much calcium has built up in the coronary arteries.
We've covered this before on the Health Report, questioning the value of a
coronary calcium score. Well, now the Baker Heart and Diabetes Institute is
starting a study in otherwise healthy people with a close family history of heart
disease at a relatively young age. The person leading the study is Tom Marwick
who is the Baker Institute's director, and he's in our Melbourne studio. Welcome
to the Health Report, Tom.

Tom Marwick: Hi Norman, thanks for the invitation.

Norman Swan: So what's the question you're trying to answer here?

Tom Marwick: Well, it really arises from clinical interaction. I quite often see
people who have a family history of heart disease. They may come in to say that
their father died at the age of 58 and they are in their early 50s and what should
they do. And obviously in that situation you need to ask the patient carefully
about symptoms, and sometimes they actually have symptoms that they haven't
admitted to anybody previously, and then you treat that on its own merits. But
many individuals are truly asymptomatic and then you calculate their risk using a
risk calculator.

Norman Swan: So just to explain that, that brings together your family history,
whether you smoke, your blood pressure, your cholesterol levels and various
 
other factors, and then you get a score, your percentage chance of a heart attack
in the next five or 10 years.

Tom Marwick: Yes, that's right, and that's what you would do really for a routine
over the age of 40 check. And then you can identify some people at very low risk
and a few people at very high risk, and then there's a group in between at
intermediate risk where you are really trying to balance up the fact that they
haven't got a very high risk of disease but they have a family history. And
unfortunately the risk calculators don't take family history into account. So it's a
frequent problem and it's a source of frustration to all I think.

Norman Swan: And that's where you are testing this ground of the coronary
calcium score.

Tom Marwick: Yes, so our plan was to take these people with a family history,
do a coronary calcium score on them. If they had a score of between zero and
400, then to randomise them to a study with a statin or none. People over the
score of 400 clearly have coronary disease…

Norman Swan: So this is like a cut-off when you talk about the 400?

Tom Marwick: Yes, so the score is derived from the total extent of calcium in the
vasculature, and it's kind of a reflection of the amount of atherosclerosis in the
arteries. And a score of 400 is a meaningful score prognostically and warrants
some further evaluation, perhaps a stress test. Very commonly that's negative,
but those individuals I think you could make a pretty strong argument to treat
them with a statin. The individuals with a calcium score of zero have got a very
low risk. It's a very reassuring finding. And the people in the middle, it's very
difficult to know what to do with them.

Norman Swan: We first covered this years ago when it first came on the market
and before the studies were done, and it was thought it was pretty useless, that
you could have a zero coronary calcium score and drop down dead of a heart
attack the next day. But I think this CT scans have improved since then. But
nowadays you've got what are called CT coronary angiograms, which are fairly
benign tests, check your coronary arteries. If they are clean as a whistle, off you
go, and if it finds something then you can go on to, say, having a stress echo or
 
something like that. With the CT coronary angiogram available to you, why would
you bother doing the coronary calcium?

Tom Marwick: I think they are giving different signals. I think when you do the
CT coronary angiogram you are looking for the presence of obstructive disease.
And when you are doing…

Norman Swan: But isn't that what you are looking for in the coronary calcium
score too?

Tom Marwick: No, absolutely not, no, you are looking for evidence of
atherosclerotic plaque in the coronary arteries. So if you find a coronary calcium
score of zero, those individuals are extremely unlikely to have plaque in the
coronaries.

Norman Swan: And probably just the missing bit here for the audience is that
calcium lands there and sticks from the blood supply as a kind of marker of the
plaque, of the cholesterol plaque.

Tom Marwick: Yes, absolutely, so it's a disease marker rather than a risk factor,
absolutely. So this isn't something that is bad about calcium that comes to sit in
your coronary arteries and cause mischief, it's a bystander in the disease
process, but it's a marker of the disease, yes.

Norman Swan: So what have you found so far? I realise the trial is just getting
going.

Tom Marwick: So we've been going actually for a couple of years, a multicentre
study really in all of the capital cities. And we obviously have follow-up to do for
several years more. But we do have the baseline data. And it's very interesting
that these folk who are at intermediate risk with a family history of premature
disease, I would have thought that those individuals would be very likely to have
evidence of coronary disease, in fact 50% of them have had a score of zero.

Norman Swan: 50%?

Tom Marwick: Yes, a very reassuring result.
 
Norman Swan: Is that because they are scared as hell and they are living
pristine lives?

Tom Marwick: Well, I don't know. I suppose there is a significant genetic
component to this disease, and I suppose their lives aren't that pristine, because
they are at intermediate risk, so they've got an elevated cholesterol or they
smoke or have high blood pressure. So no, I don't think so. I think the message
from this is that there is actually a different signal from the coronary calcium
score than we are getting from the coronary risk evaluation. I think maybe it's a
reflection of the protective process, that you can expose two people to the same
levels of risk factors so one of them develops coronary disease and the other
does not.

Norman Swan: And time will tell whether intervening makes a difference.

Tom Marwick: Absolutely, yes, I think, as you said in the introduction, I think
we've jumped the gun on this, and people are being managed as though we have
proven this, but in fact we haven't. We have shown that the presence of calcium
is a marker of disease, and we've shown that it's a marker of prognosis, but we
have not shown that by intervening that we can change the outcome, and this
trial will show that for the first time.

Norman Swan: And you're looking for people with first or second degree
relatives with early premature heart disease. How do they participate in the trial if
they want to?

Tom Marwick: Yes, so all they need to do is to go to the Baker Institute website
and look under 'patients' and there is a list of trials there and the trial is called
CAUGHT-CAD for coronary artery disease.

Norman Swan: And all you need to do is have a CT scan of the heart. Tom,
thank you very much for joining us.

Tom Marwick: My pleasure, thank you.

Norman Swan: Tom Marwick is director of the Baker Heart and Diabetes
Institute in Melbourne.
 
Generic medicines are cheaper versions of branded medications once they have
come out of patent and can be made and sold by other companies. Governments
rely on generics to keep costs down, but most generics are of drugs which are
relatively simple chemicals to manufacture, like statins, for example. But the most
expensive drugs on the market these days are so-called biologics, they are very
complex, usually antibodies designed to block very specific lock and key
mechanisms in cells. They cost tens of thousands of dollars a year and the
patent holders have been hoping that it will be too hard for generic companies to
design them. A recent study though showed a so-called biosimilar performed well
compared to the branded product, in this case Herceptin for women with breast
cancer. One of the researchers was Hope Rugo, director of the breast oncology
at the University of California San Francisco's Comprehensive Cancer Centre.
Welcome to the Health Report.

Hope Rugo: Thanks for having me.

Norman Swan: This is a big story, isn't it, that a biosimilar has actually had a
randomised trial? Because the pharmaceutical industry is saying you can't copy
our drugs and we are going to have the market for ever.

Hope Rugo: I think it's very exciting. And actually went this paper came out I had
a sudden realisation that what I went into medicine for as a starry-eyed less than
10-year-old, which was to sort of help the world, that this was maybe the closest I
had gotten to it. You know, that by helping these people do a study which will, we
expect, lead to approval of a biosimilar for trastuzumab will improve access to
this lifesaving antibody worldwide. A lot of this is going to be due to the
development of competition. The drug costs will come down.

Norman Swan: So just tell us about the biosimilar. The trade name of the drug
that is not the biosimilar, the original one, is Herceptin, and this is really one of
the first targeted drugs in cancer and aimed at breast cancer, but probably other
cancers as well. What is the biosimilar?

Hope Rugo: In the late '80s there was an identification that a gene could be
amplified or increased in number in some cancers called HER-2 or Rb2. And
over the next decade an antibody was developed against that receptor, we call it
a targeted biologic therapy. And what has really been amazing over the last 20
 
years is that from the development of that antibody until now, most women can
be cured of HER-2 positive early stage breast cancer by using that antibody,
Herceptin or trastuzumab, and another one which is added to it. And we
understand that adding these antibodies to chemotherapy really improves
survival, even in patients with incurable breast cancer, and it improves survival
for a median of a year and a half even or two years. So it's really a big deal. So
the idea behind the biosimilar is that you are taking a biologic product, this
antibody, and making a drug that is very similar to it, but clinically how the drug is
cleared, whether you make antibodies to it, all these other kind of biochemical
tests that are done in the laboratory and in animals, that the drug is similar to
another of a degree that you don't see differences in its clinical activity or its side-
effects.

Norman Swan: So what were the results of this randomised trial?

Hope Rugo: So this randomised trial showed that if you have developed
recurrent breast cancer that fit this criteria, it is HER-2 positive, which is about
20% to 25% of breast cancer, and you are randomised to receive a
chemotherapy drug plus either the branded Herceptin or this proposed biosimilar,
the results in terms of response to the treatment and then the duration of
response to treatment are identical. In addition there were no differences in
toxicity.

Norman Swan: Response rates meaning the tumour shrinks, you get an
observable response. But what counts for women is years of survival. Do you
have any comparative data on that?

Hope Rugo: That data has existed since the first trials came out using Herceptin,
the branded trastuzumab. So this drug because it has been similar with the other
criteria will be expected to be similar with survival as well. So you could say, well,
I get to choose, I'm not stuck with this one antibody, and I can use one of those
two antibodies, so I can actually bargain to get the best deal. Hopefully the
biosimilars will be at a substantial enough discount so that more people will be
able to afford longer therapy.

One of the problems with targeted therapy, and this is across the board in
treating cancer, is that you give it for a long time when it works well, so then the
 
costs just keep building up. So you really need it to be less expensive, because
you are not just getting it for three months. If it works…you know, I have patients
who have been on branded Herceptin for a decade.

Norman Swan: Which is several hundred thousand dollars, if not more.

Hope Rugo: A bit more.

Norman Swan: A few weeks ago in Australia the highest cost drug list was
published and it was very different from the list of drugs that are most commonly
prescribed. And a lot of them were these monoclonal antibody drugs for
autoimmune disease for cancer and other things. So more and more are coming
on, and they generally cost $60,000, $80,000, sometimes even $100,000 a year.
How generalisable are the findings from this particular monoclonal antibody, the
trastuzumab, to other monoclonal antibody drugs which are costing health
systems around the world a fortune?

Hope Rugo: Well, I think this is a whole new era. I think one of the key things to
remember is that the branded drug has to reach the end of its patent to be able
to sell these drugs in most countries. There are biosimilars that are on the market
now for autoimmune diseases, there is a biosimilar marketed and approved in
the United States for a growth factor that helps white blood cells stay strong
during chemotherapy. This will be the first antibody for the treatment of cancer,
and I think what it's going to do is open a floodgate of studies and approvals for
other antibodies. For example, there was a study looking at another antibody we
don't use in the breast cancer but is used in a number of other cancers,
bevacizumab or Avastin, and that study also showed similarity so that that cost
can also be reduced.

Norman Swan: But essentially what we are talking about here is the potential for
generics in the monoclonal antibody market.

Hope Rugo: Yes. You know, you asked about survival, and it's a really
interesting thing, a lot of people have asked about endpoints, so can you show
that the survival is the same? But it's important to keep in mind that the
regulatory agencies developed the criteria for establishing biosimilarity, keeping
in mind that if you require all of the same steps as the originator product, it's
 
going to cost the same amount. So what you want to do is to get a drug that is
similar by the main criteria.

Norman Swan: Thank you very much for joining us on the Health Report.

Hope Rugo: A pleasure to be here, and thanks for your interest.

Norman Swan: Hope Rugo who is director of breast oncology at the University
of California San Francisco's Comprehensive Cancer Centre.

I'm Norman Swan, this has been the Health Report, do join me next week.

pages.text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, the value or not of having what's called your coronary
calcium score measured on a CT scan. It has been a money-maker for years, the
question is whether it's worth doing. A trial of common painkillers comparing their
ability to cause heart attacks. A way to bring down the cost and perhaps increase
the availability of some of the most expensive cancer drugs. And two trials which
suggests that an automated online therapy program for insomnia works, and
there's a strong Australian connection. The person who has led the project for
some years is Lee Ritterband, professor of psychiatry and neurobehavioural
sciences at the University of Virginia. Welcome to the Health Report.

Lee Ritterband: Thanks for having me.

Norman Swan: So how do you define insomnia?

Lee Ritterband: Difficulty falling asleep, waking up in the middle of the night not
being able to get back to sleep, waking too early in the morning or just not feeling
like you've had a good night's sleep.

Norman Swan: But the message here is that you are bothered by it, because
some people might have the same sort of issues but they are not bothered by it.

Lee Ritterband: That's right, absolutely.

Norman Swan: And where did the idea that cognitive behavioural therapy might
work for insomnia…? Because you'd think, well, you're waking up so why bother?
What's going to make a difference to your sleep if you are told to think differently
about it?

Lee Ritterband: Well, cognitive behavioural therapy is a general approach that
actually has been found to be pretty efficacious in a number of different areas,
and insomnia and sleep happen to be one of them that it is particularly good at
addressing. It focuses on how we think and how we feel and the connection
between the two. And what we find is that a lot of the difficulties that people have
with their sleep are wrapped up in how they are thinking about their sleep and the
anxiety that revolves around their sleep, and so there is some cognitive work that
focuses on thinking differently about how we sleep. And the behaviour piece is

really focused on implementing certain rules and guidelines and strategies that
can improve the actual process of sleep.

Norman Swan: So-called sleep hygiene, that's the bed is just for sleeping and
sex, and not for working and not for watching television, and go to bed at the
same time each night and don't have coffee before you go to bed and that sort of
thing.

Lee Ritterband: That's right. Actually you combine both the sleep hygiene as
well as the stimulus control strategies. There are three areas in there, there's
sleep hygiene which is a lot of the things people already know; don't drink coffee
close to bed, don't exercise close to bed, some of those issues. There are the
stimulus control techniques that we are trying to disconnect the body's tendency
to be awake when in bed and not sleep. And so there is an attempt to modify that
through some rules, which is what the stimulus control rules are.

And then there is this third piece which is sleep restriction, which is a bit
paradoxical in the sense that we actually restrict people's sleep initially in order to
improve the efficiency of their sleep. And so what we see is that a lot of folks
come in with really poor sleep efficiency. And we calculate sleep efficiency by
looking at what percentage of time are people asleep when they are in bed. So if
I'm sleeping for five hours a night but I'm in bed for 10 hours, then I have a 50%
sleep efficiency, and we really want to get people up over 85%. And to do that we
will often encourage a shorter period of time of being in bed to sleep as a way of
consolidating sleep during that period.

Norman Swan: And the stimulus control?

Lee Ritterband: The stimulus control are the rules that you were starting to
mention before, you know, only use the bed for sleep and sex, don't watch
television or do other things in bed, you get out of bed if you are not asleep within
20 minutes. All of those rules are put in place in order to break the connection of
being awake when in bed.

Norman Swan: You've been one of the international pioneers, along with Helen
Christensen at the Black Dog and others, of online therapy. So you instituted this
as an online piece where you didn't actually have a therapist, you did this as part
of an online program called SHUTi. Just tell us a little bit about this study.

Lee Ritterband: The study was looking at the use of this online program SHUTi,
and following people over a period of a year to see how well does the
intervention…and this is a fully automated, interactive, tailored program, there is
no human support involved in it. And we wanted to see if we gave this to people,
if we had them use it, how well would it work over a longer period of time. And we
looked at people right after they used it, at six months after they used it and then
at one year to see how they were doing.

Norman Swan: And how did they go?

Lee Ritterband: Great, just really strong, positive, robust outcomes. We've done
a number of studies with SHUTi now over the last few years, and this study was
particularly of interest because we were really opening it up to a lot of different
kinds of people, people who had already different issues that were going on,
psychiatric issues like depression or anxiety as well as medical problems,
whether they had asthma or cancer or other medical problems. Over 50% of the
people who were in this trial had one or both of those kinds of issues. And so we
really wanted to see if SHUTi worked in this real-world setting. And the findings
were as strong as we've ever seen.

Norman Swan: So, faster to sleep, longer sleeping times, that sort of thing?

Lee Ritterband: Yes, faster to sleep, not being awake as long in the middle of
the night, having much improved sleep. In fact over half of the group who got
SHUTi were what we call treatment remitters, they were not having any insomnia
anymore at one year.

Norman Swan: And you did another study with Helen Christensen at the Black
Dog and others at the ANU and Sydney University looking at people with
depression. What was the findings there?

Lee Ritterband: Yes, that was a fantastic study. We recruited over 1,000 people
in Australia, and everybody in that trial had insomnia but were also at risk for
major depression. And what we found was that if we treated those who had
insomnia and were at risk for major depression, that we could not only
significantly improve their sleep, which we did, but we also significantly
decreased their depressive aspect, they were not feeling as depressed anymore.
Insomnia and depression definitely are comorbid, they often come together.

Sometimes depression leads to the insomnia, sometimes the insomnia leads to
the depression, and oftentimes they are just comorbid, meaning that they happen
around the same time.

Norman Swan: You're not the only program that offers cognitive behavioural
therapy for insomnia. How does yours rate with the others?

Lee Ritterband: Yes, there are some other programs, and there are some that
have good data. But the concern is that people who are looking to consume
these programs, is to really make sure that the program is that they want to buy
or to use have some real evidence base behind them, but nothing comes close to
the robustness of the data that we see with SHUTi.

Norman Swan: And if you want it in Australia you can get it via the Black Dog
Institute?

Lee Ritterband: You can, you can go to the Black Dog Institute's webpage and
they should have a box there, a link there that you can select to go and get
SHUTi right from there.

Norman Swan: And there is a charge for SHUTi, by the way. Lee Ritterbrand is
professor of psychiatry and neurobehavioural sciences at the University of
Virginia.

And you're listening to the Health Report here on RN, at ABC News Radio and
CBC Radio across Canada. I'm Norman Swan.

Some of the commonest painkillers bought across the counter are called non-
steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or NSAIDs, medications like ibuprofen or
naproxen, their trade names are Nurofen or Naprosyn. There's been a suspicion
that in some people they may increase the risk of a heart attack, particularly a
newer supposedly lower risk NSAID called celecoxib, Celebrex. Well, now a
huge trial has been published comparing these three NSAIDs and their heart
risks, and one of the authors was Professor Neville Yeomans of Western Sydney
University and the Austin Hospital in Melbourne and he joins me in the studio
now. Welcome Neville.

Neville Yeomans: Glad to be with you Norman.

Norman Swan: It's a huge study.

Neville Yeomans: Yes, it took a long while, it's been a lot of work, but at the end
of the day I think it has been worth it.

Norman Swan: So let's just talk about why do NSAIDs, in theory, increase the
risk of a heart attack?

Neville Yeomans: You know, that in itself, I think that theory is pretty muddied.
But more to the point they did appear that they do increase the risk a little bit. If I
just wind back a tiny bit, the problem with the NSAIDs that I think most people
know is they do cause some damage to the gut and can cause a bleeding ulcer.
So when it was worked out that there was one molecule they blocked that is bad
for the stomach and the other one they block is good for the pain and
inflammation, that's when the selective COX-2 NSAIDs were developed.

Norman Swan: And that's what celecoxib is.

Neville Yeomans: That's right.

Norman Swan: And infamously there was a sister drug called rofecoxib.

Neville Yeomans: Right, and you are bringing me really to what was the main
source of the concern. In a big study…because these drugs seemed generally
pretty safe and were likely to cause less ulcers and less bleeding, both Celebrex
and rofecoxib were trialled to try to prevent bowel cancer. The irony is that both
of them showed benefit in that. But after about 18 months in two of the studies
and not the third there began to be slightly more heart attacks. And it got to the
extent with rofecoxib of being about twice as much. It could have been chance
but it seemed unlikely to be chance, so there was suddenly concern about the
whole family of them.

Norman Swan: And there was an element of hiding the results, and rofecoxib
ended up getting taken off the market.

Neville Yeomans: Some of that is true actually, and it was perhaps almost
surprising that Celebrex remained, although it did appear to have rather different
properties. And what we also know now is that probably all of the NSAIDs slightly

increase the risk of a heart attack, and we didn't know that because in the old
days they were never tested to the same level.

Norman Swan: So Pfizer, the drug company, funded this study to compare
Celebrex against two other common ones, ibuprofen and naproxen.

Neville Yeomans: Yes, I think they really were planning to look into this anyway,
in fact I know they were, with a study they didn't go ahead with. But then the
Food and Drug Administration in the States said, look, this is a concern, and so
they mandated the study, and Pfizer then had no choice. It's been a big and
expensive exercise.

Norman Swan: And you were independent of the drug company?

Neville Yeomans: We were. In fact the steering committee…in fact interestingly
every member of the executive committee every year signed an affidavit that they
would take no finance from any maker of any NSAIDs.

Norman Swan: So what did you find?

Neville Yeomans: Well, the key thing was; was there going to be difference in
cardiovascular deaths?

Norman Swan: And these are people with rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis,
they were taking it for pain relief for their arthritis?

Neville Yeomans: Absolutely, they had proven that they needed it, they had
been on it for at least six months, it was judged that they needed to continue with
it for up to three or four years, and they were told that one of the drugs might
increase their risk of a heart attack. So that was brave people to tackle it. The
primary endpoint was just that; was there an increased risk of cardiac death,
acute myocardial infarction, that is heart attack, and acute stroke? It was the first
time I've been involved with what's called a non-inferiority trial where you start
from the very beginning to plan the study on the assumption that there will be a
difference and you want to find out if there is. Normally you are doing things in
the reverse order. The answer, to cut to the chase, was that perhaps almost to
the surprise of some of us there was no difference between the three NSAIDs in
cardiac risk. There was actually a trend to slightly less on the one that is safer for

the stomach. And perhaps most importantly there was a one-third reduction in
all-cause mortality that was statistically significant.

Norman Swan: So was that from bowel cancer or what?

Neville Yeomans: No, most of them will have been cardiovascular, renal,
GI…look, I can't actually tell you the full breakdown of the deaths.

Norman Swan: But it could have been a few things.

Neville Yeomans: Oh yes, there would have been others.

Norman Swan: But there have been other studies which show that ibuprofen
does raise the risk of…so in other words what you didn't answer was if you didn't
take any NSAIDs, would you have had a lower risk of a heart attack or stroke?

Neville Yeomans: That's a really good question, and to really answer it well
would be a randomised trial where you put somebody on a placebo for three
years who had an increased risk of heart disease and had bad joints, and no one
could ever do that, so we have to fall back on epidemiologic studies. And the
epidemiology suggests there is probably a slight increase with all of them.
There's one study that is just under review at the moment from Québec province
where they've got wonderful data linkage that said that the increase in risk…it's
probably a bit unfair for me to say this because it hasn't gone through a full peer
review, but I've got this far to say it looked like about a 10% increase with
celecoxib and a little bit more with most of the others. But these aren't poison,
this is not like smoking and lung cancer.

Norman Swan: What's a person to do? They've got arthritis and let's say they've
got high cholesterol, the doctor has told them they are at high risk of heart
disease. Is it safe to go and buy one of these off the counter?

Neville Yeomans: Look, I think based on what we have found, if it were me I
would be inclined to take one of them by prescription, that means your doctor is
looking after you closely. Oh, I should say that all of these patients were taking
an antiulcer drug which adds a little expense but also made the whole thing
safer. So if they've got bad joints they've got to do something for pain, and if they
can't exercise that's bad for the heart. I think it's important to control pain.

Norman Swan: So just get it in balance. And the celecoxib had lower risk of
stomach problems but it wasn't so good for pain relief, that was the other thing.

Neville Yeomans: Yes, maybe so. There was a slight difference against one of
the other two drugs and not the other, so yes, fair comment.

Norman Swan: Neville, thank you very much for joining us.

Neville Yeomans: It's been a pleasure.

Norman Swan: Neville Yeomans who is director of research at the Austin
Hospital in Melbourne.

The Australian healthcare system and often you and me as consumers spend a
fortune on testing to see whether we have heart disease or are at risk of a heart
attack. One such test is called a coronary calcium score and involves a CT scan
of the heart looking at how much calcium has built up in the coronary arteries.
We've covered this before on the Health Report, questioning the value of a
coronary calcium score. Well, now the Baker Heart and Diabetes Institute is
starting a study in otherwise healthy people with a close family history of heart
disease at a relatively young age. The person leading the study is Tom Marwick
who is the Baker Institute's director, and he's in our Melbourne studio. Welcome
to the Health Report, Tom.

Tom Marwick: Hi Norman, thanks for the invitation.

Norman Swan: So what's the question you're trying to answer here?

Tom Marwick: Well, it really arises from clinical interaction. I quite often see
people who have a family history of heart disease. They may come in to say that
their father died at the age of 58 and they are in their early 50s and what should
they do. And obviously in that situation you need to ask the patient carefully
about symptoms, and sometimes they actually have symptoms that they haven't
admitted to anybody previously, and then you treat that on its own merits. But
many individuals are truly asymptomatic and then you calculate their risk using a
risk calculator.

Norman Swan: So just to explain that, that brings together your family history,
whether you smoke, your blood pressure, your cholesterol levels and various

other factors, and then you get a score, your percentage chance of a heart attack
in the next five or 10 years.

Tom Marwick: Yes, that's right, and that's what you would do really for a routine
over the age of 40 check. And then you can identify some people at very low risk
and a few people at very high risk, and then there's a group in between at
intermediate risk where you are really trying to balance up the fact that they
haven't got a very high risk of disease but they have a family history. And
unfortunately the risk calculators don't take family history into account. So it's a
frequent problem and it's a source of frustration to all I think.

Norman Swan: And that's where you are testing this ground of the coronary
calcium score.

Tom Marwick: Yes, so our plan was to take these people with a family history,
do a coronary calcium score on them. If they had a score of between zero and
400, then to randomise them to a study with a statin or none. People over the
score of 400 clearly have coronary disease…

Norman Swan: So this is like a cut-off when you talk about the 400?

Tom Marwick: Yes, so the score is derived from the total extent of calcium in the
vasculature, and it's kind of a reflection of the amount of atherosclerosis in the
arteries. And a score of 400 is a meaningful score prognostically and warrants
some further evaluation, perhaps a stress test. Very commonly that's negative,
but those individuals I think you could make a pretty strong argument to treat
them with a statin. The individuals with a calcium score of zero have got a very
low risk. It's a very reassuring finding. And the people in the middle, it's very
difficult to know what to do with them.

Norman Swan: We first covered this years ago when it first came on the market
and before the studies were done, and it was thought it was pretty useless, that
you could have a zero coronary calcium score and drop down dead of a heart
attack the next day. But I think this CT scans have improved since then. But
nowadays you've got what are called CT coronary angiograms, which are fairly
benign tests, check your coronary arteries. If they are clean as a whistle, off you
go, and if it finds something then you can go on to, say, having a stress echo or

something like that. With the CT coronary angiogram available to you, why would
you bother doing the coronary calcium?

Tom Marwick: I think they are giving different signals. I think when you do the
CT coronary angiogram you are looking for the presence of obstructive disease.
And when you are doing…

Norman Swan: But isn't that what you are looking for in the coronary calcium
score too?

Tom Marwick: No, absolutely not, no, you are looking for evidence of
atherosclerotic plaque in the coronary arteries. So if you find a coronary calcium
score of zero, those individuals are extremely unlikely to have plaque in the
coronaries.

Norman Swan: And probably just the missing bit here for the audience is that
calcium lands there and sticks from the blood supply as a kind of marker of the
plaque, of the cholesterol plaque.

Tom Marwick: Yes, absolutely, so it's a disease marker rather than a risk factor,
absolutely. So this isn't something that is bad about calcium that comes to sit in
your coronary arteries and cause mischief, it's a bystander in the disease
process, but it's a marker of the disease, yes.

Norman Swan: So what have you found so far? I realise the trial is just getting
going.

Tom Marwick: So we've been going actually for a couple of years, a multicentre
study really in all of the capital cities. And we obviously have follow-up to do for
several years more. But we do have the baseline data. And it's very interesting
that these folk who are at intermediate risk with a family history of premature
disease, I would have thought that those individuals would be very likely to have
evidence of coronary disease, in fact 50% of them have had a score of zero.

Norman Swan: 50%?

Tom Marwick: Yes, a very reassuring result.

Norman Swan: Is that because they are scared as hell and they are living
pristine lives?

Tom Marwick: Well, I don't know. I suppose there is a significant genetic
component to this disease, and I suppose their lives aren't that pristine, because
they are at intermediate risk, so they've got an elevated cholesterol or they
smoke or have high blood pressure. So no, I don't think so. I think the message
from this is that there is actually a different signal from the coronary calcium
score than we are getting from the coronary risk evaluation. I think maybe it's a
reflection of the protective process, that you can expose two people to the same
levels of risk factors so one of them develops coronary disease and the other
does not.

Norman Swan: And time will tell whether intervening makes a difference.

Tom Marwick: Absolutely, yes, I think, as you said in the introduction, I think
we've jumped the gun on this, and people are being managed as though we have
proven this, but in fact we haven't. We have shown that the presence of calcium
is a marker of disease, and we've shown that it's a marker of prognosis, but we
have not shown that by intervening that we can change the outcome, and this
trial will show that for the first time.

Norman Swan: And you're looking for people with first or second degree
relatives with early premature heart disease. How do they participate in the trial if
they want to?

Tom Marwick: Yes, so all they need to do is to go to the Baker Institute website
and look under 'patients' and there is a list of trials there and the trial is called
CAUGHT-CAD for coronary artery disease.

Norman Swan: And all you need to do is have a CT scan of the heart. Tom,
thank you very much for joining us.

Tom Marwick: My pleasure, thank you.

Norman Swan: Tom Marwick is director of the Baker Heart and Diabetes
Institute in Melbourne.

Generic medicines are cheaper versions of branded medications once they have
come out of patent and can be made and sold by other companies. Governments
rely on generics to keep costs down, but most generics are of drugs which are
relatively simple chemicals to manufacture, like statins, for example. But the most
expensive drugs on the market these days are so-called biologics, they are very
complex, usually antibodies designed to block very specific lock and key
mechanisms in cells. They cost tens of thousands of dollars a year and the
patent holders have been hoping that it will be too hard for generic companies to
design them. A recent study though showed a so-called biosimilar performed well
compared to the branded product, in this case Herceptin for women with breast
cancer. One of the researchers was Hope Rugo, director of the breast oncology
at the University of California San Francisco's Comprehensive Cancer Centre.
Welcome to the Health Report.

Hope Rugo: Thanks for having me.

Norman Swan: This is a big story, isn't it, that a biosimilar has actually had a
randomised trial? Because the pharmaceutical industry is saying you can't copy
our drugs and we are going to have the market for ever.

Hope Rugo: I think it's very exciting. And actually went this paper came out I had
a sudden realisation that what I went into medicine for as a starry-eyed less than
10-year-old, which was to sort of help the world, that this was maybe the closest I
had gotten to it. You know, that by helping these people do a study which will, we
expect, lead to approval of a biosimilar for trastuzumab will improve access to
this lifesaving antibody worldwide. A lot of this is going to be due to the
development of competition. The drug costs will come down.

Norman Swan: So just tell us about the biosimilar. The trade name of the drug
that is not the biosimilar, the original one, is Herceptin, and this is really one of
the first targeted drugs in cancer and aimed at breast cancer, but probably other
cancers as well. What is the biosimilar?

Hope Rugo: In the late '80s there was an identification that a gene could be
amplified or increased in number in some cancers called HER-2 or Rb2. And
over the next decade an antibody was developed against that receptor, we call it
a targeted biologic therapy. And what has really been amazing over the last 20

years is that from the development of that antibody until now, most women can
be cured of HER-2 positive early stage breast cancer by using that antibody,
Herceptin or trastuzumab, and another one which is added to it. And we
understand that adding these antibodies to chemotherapy really improves
survival, even in patients with incurable breast cancer, and it improves survival
for a median of a year and a half even or two years. So it's really a big deal. So
the idea behind the biosimilar is that you are taking a biologic product, this
antibody, and making a drug that is very similar to it, but clinically how the drug is
cleared, whether you make antibodies to it, all these other kind of biochemical
tests that are done in the laboratory and in animals, that the drug is similar to
another of a degree that you don't see differences in its clinical activity or its side-
effects.

Norman Swan: So what were the results of this randomised trial?

Hope Rugo: So this randomised trial showed that if you have developed
recurrent breast cancer that fit this criteria, it is HER-2 positive, which is about
20% to 25% of breast cancer, and you are randomised to receive a
chemotherapy drug plus either the branded Herceptin or this proposed biosimilar,
the results in terms of response to the treatment and then the duration of
response to treatment are identical. In addition there were no differences in
toxicity.

Norman Swan: Response rates meaning the tumour shrinks, you get an
observable response. But what counts for women is years of survival. Do you
have any comparative data on that?

Hope Rugo: That data has existed since the first trials came out using Herceptin,
the branded trastuzumab. So this drug because it has been similar with the other
criteria will be expected to be similar with survival as well. So you could say, well,
I get to choose, I'm not stuck with this one antibody, and I can use one of those
two antibodies, so I can actually bargain to get the best deal. Hopefully the
biosimilars will be at a substantial enough discount so that more people will be
able to afford longer therapy.

One of the problems with targeted therapy, and this is across the board in
treating cancer, is that you give it for a long time when it works well, so then the

costs just keep building up. So you really need it to be less expensive, because
you are not just getting it for three months. If it works…you know, I have patients
who have been on branded Herceptin for a decade.

Norman Swan: Which is several hundred thousand dollars, if not more.

Hope Rugo: A bit more.

Norman Swan: A few weeks ago in Australia the highest cost drug list was
published and it was very different from the list of drugs that are most commonly
prescribed. And a lot of them were these monoclonal antibody drugs for
autoimmune disease for cancer and other things. So more and more are coming
on, and they generally cost $60,000, $80,000, sometimes even $100,000 a year.
How generalisable are the findings from this particular monoclonal antibody, the
trastuzumab, to other monoclonal antibody drugs which are costing health
systems around the world a fortune?

Hope Rugo: Well, I think this is a whole new era. I think one of the key things to
remember is that the branded drug has to reach the end of its patent to be able
to sell these drugs in most countries. There are biosimilars that are on the market
now for autoimmune diseases, there is a biosimilar marketed and approved in
the United States for a growth factor that helps white blood cells stay strong
during chemotherapy. This will be the first antibody for the treatment of cancer,
and I think what it's going to do is open a floodgate of studies and approvals for
other antibodies. For example, there was a study looking at another antibody we
don't use in the breast cancer but is used in a number of other cancers,
bevacizumab or Avastin, and that study also showed similarity so that that cost
can also be reduced.

Norman Swan: But essentially what we are talking about here is the potential for
generics in the monoclonal antibody market.

Hope Rugo: Yes. You know, you asked about survival, and it's a really
interesting thing, a lot of people have asked about endpoints, so can you show
that the survival is the same? But it's important to keep in mind that the
regulatory agencies developed the criteria for establishing biosimilarity, keeping
in mind that if you require all of the same steps as the originator product, it's

going to cost the same amount. So what you want to do is to get a drug that is
similar by the main criteria.

Norman Swan: Thank you very much for joining us on the Health Report.

Hope Rugo: A pleasure to be here, and thanks for your interest.

Norman Swan: Hope Rugo who is director of breast oncology at the University
of California San Francisco's Comprehensive Cancer Centre.

I'm Norman Swan, this has been the Health Report, do join me next week.
